issues.legal_issue: An isolated loan transaction outside the lender’s regular money-lending business in a district is not barred or invalidated merely because the lender lacks a registration certificate for that district.
material_facts: The lender regularly carried on money-lending business in one district and held a valid certificate for that district.
The lender made a single loan in another district, where the borrowers’ property securing the loan was situated, but did not carry on a regular money-lending business.
The lender sued to recover the loan on the mortgages, and the borrowers argued that the absence of a certificate for the second district made the transaction void and the suit incompetent.
issues.conclusion: The isolated transaction was outside the prohibitions in sections 11-F and 11-H of the C.P. and Berar Moneylenders’ Act, 1934. It was not invalidated for want of a certificate for that district, and the suit could proceed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(v), a moneylender is a person who advances loans in the regular course of business. Section 11-F prohibits carrying on the business of money-lending in a district without a valid certificate for that district; it does not prohibit or invalidate an isolated loan outside that business. Section 11-H likewise does not prevent a suit concerning such an isolated transaction. The statutory scheme regulates the business of money-lending rather than individual transactions; section 11-G’s provision for composition of offences supports that interpretation. The Court approved Patiram v. Baliram, Hajarimal v. Hari Narayan and Janki Bai v. Ratan Melu, and distinguished Cornelius v. Phillips because the English and Indian statutory schemes were not identical. It also relied on Sitaram Sharwan v. Bajya Parnay for the meaning of “regular course of business” and noted the Privy Council’s caution in Lasa Din v. Mt. Gulab Kunwar against applying English decisions to Indian statutes.

rule.if: loan_recovery_suit and isolated_loan_transaction and not regular_lending_in_district

predicates.loan_recovery_suit: A party brings a civil suit to recover a loan.
predicates.isolated_loan_transaction: The lender made a loan as an isolated transaction rather than as part of a regular course of money-lending business in the relevant district.
predicates.regular_lending_in_district: The lender regularly carried on the business of advancing loans in the relevant district.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks recovery of an isolated loan made outside the lender’s regular money-lending business in the district, the loan remains enforceable and the suit may proceed without a certificate for that district.

issues.legal_issue: A long-standing judicial interpretation of an ambiguous statute should not be displaced without exceptional reason when people have relied on it and it is not clearly erroneous.
material_facts: Several courts had adopted the interpretation that the registration requirement regulated the business of money-lending and did not invalidate isolated transactions.
The interpretation had prevailed for a considerable period, during which people had arranged property dealings and contracts in reliance on it.
The challenged interpretation was not patently erroneous, the breach of the registration requirement was a penal offence, and legislative amendments had not changed the relevant requirement.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to overturn the established interpretation and applied it to the dispute.
issues.legal_principle: Where statutory language is ambiguous and a higher court’s interpretation has stood for a considerable period, courts ordinarily should not adopt a materially different interpretation that would unsettle transactions made in reliance on the established view, absent exceptional reason. The Court also regarded the penal consequence of contravention and the legislature’s decision not to amend the relevant provision, despite amending other provisions, as reasons for caution. It relied on the established interpretations in Patiram v. Baliram, Janki Bai v. Ratan Melu and Hajarimal v. Hari Narayan.

predicates.appeal_seeks_to_overturn_settled_interpr: A party in an appeal asks the court to replace a judicial interpretation that has been applied over a considerable period.
predicates.statutory_meaning_is_ambiguous: The statutory language is capable of more than one reasonable interpretation.
predicates.settled_interpretation_relied_on_in_tran: People have arranged transactions in reliance on the interpretation adopted by the courts.
predicates.interpretation_not_clearly_erroneous: The established interpretation is not so clearly and patently erroneous that it must be rejected.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a long-standing interpretation of ambiguous statutory language on which people have relied, and that interpretation is not clearly erroneous, the interpretation is retained.

issues.legal_issue: A decree need not be altered solely to provide separate mortgage decrees when the difference is one of form and does not materially affect substantive rights.
material_facts: The suit concerned three mortgages over separate properties.
The appellants argued that the decree should consist of three separate mortgage decrees rather than one decree.
The Court considered the requested change procedural and formal, with no material effect on the parties’ substantive rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to modify the decree to provide separate mortgage decrees.
issues.legal_principle: A difference concerning the procedure or form of a decree does not warrant appellate modification when it does not materially affect the parties’ substantive rights.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party challenges a civil decree in an appeal.
predicates.decree_challenge_is_only_about_form: The requested change concerns the form or procedure of the decree rather than the underlying substantive entitlement.
predicates.form_difference_does_not_materially_affe: The difference in form does not materially change the parties’ substantive rights.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a decree is not changed solely for a difference in form when that difference does not materially affect substantive rights.
